en: During the day, land heats up faster than the ocean, causing warm air to rise and cooler sea air to rush inland to replace it.
Plant roots grow into cracks in rocks and expand as they thicken, physically breaking the solid stone into smaller pieces to form soil.
When magma cools very slowly deep underground, atoms have time to arrange into large, visible crystals, forming intrusive igneous rocks like granite.
As warm, moist air rises into the cooler upper atmosphere, the water vapor condenses around tiny dust particles to form visible cloud droplets.
Because Earth's axis is tilted, the Northern Hemisphere receives more direct sunlight during its summer months, causing warmer temperatures and longer days.
Extreme pressure and heat inside a star's core force hydrogen atoms to fuse into helium, releasing massive amounts of light and thermal energy.
The Moon's gravitational pull exerts a stronger force on the side of Earth facing it, creating an ocean water bulge that causes high tides.
When tectonic plates stuck together by friction suddenly slip and break, the released energy travels as seismic waves that shake the ground.
Dissolved gases in rising magma expand rapidly as pressure decreases near the surface, violently blowing the rock apart in an explosive volcanic eruption.
As moist wind blows over a mountain, the air rises and cools, dropping rain on the windward side and leaving the leeward side dry.
When Earth passes through dusty debris left by a comet, the particles burn up from atmospheric friction, creating a visible meteor shower.
Fungi and bacteria decompose dead leaves on the forest floor, breaking down complex organic matter into simple nutrients that plant roots can absorb.
